experiments.claim: Retry-everything duplicates effects wherever a sent write lost its outcome; a stable key removes the duplicates the provider can deduplicate; evidence-driven recovery removes them all in the measured scenarios.
experiments.hypothesis: A2: 0 scenarios with a duplicate. A0: exactly S09 S10 S11 S12 S16 S18 S19 S20 S21 S23. A1: exactly S11 S12 S18 S19 S21.
experiments.invariant: I1 and I2: at most one credit per charge, one open ticket and one message per case
limitations: Simulated providers; one deterministic run per scenario; the scenario set is coverage, not a production distribution.
experiments.question: Which runtime commits an external effect more than once when a write loses its outcome?
experiments.setup: 25 preregistered scenarios × 3 runtimes; effects counted in the simulated providers' ledgers.
experiments.title: Duplicate external effects across 25 injected faults (H1–H3)
experiments.variable: the recovery layer (A0 naive, A1 idempotent retry, A2 classified)

experiments.claim: A lost response after a committed write must not trigger a blind second execution; reconciliation by operation id resolves it.
experiments.hypothesis: A0 commits two credits; A2 commits one and dispatches once.
experiments.invariant: one credit for one duplicate charge
limitations: The idempotent runtime is also correct here because this provider honours keys: S09 alone does not separate A1 from A2.

experiments.claim: Recovery can be decided deterministically from evidence, and the decision can be checked against a frozen oracle.
experiments.hypothesis: 25 of 25 decision sequences equal the oracle; every decision recomputes from the matrix.
limitations: The oracle was written by the same author as the matrix; it checks consistency with the preregistered policy, not that the policy is optimal.
experiments.question: Does the classified runtime choose the preregistered (class, certainty, action) sequence in every scenario?
experiments.setup: experiments/scenarios.toml decisions, frozen before the run; config/recovery-matrix.toml.

experiments.claim: Caution did not cost completions: the classified runtime completed every scenario the oracle marks completable, escalated only where required, and its answers matched the ledgers.
experiments.hypothesis: A2 completes 21 of 21; escalates exactly S12 S13 S19; 0 false claims. A0 and A1 each make at least one false claim.
limitations: A production workload with more tools lacking keys and status queries would escalate more; escalation cost is a person's time, not measured.

claims.statement: A generic failure signal is insufficient for safe recovery: the runtime that treated every failure alike duplicated effects, retried refusals and made a false claim.

Failure classification distinguishes operationally different conditions: every failure the classified runtime met carried a specific class and a certainty, and no stated certainty was contradicted by the provider.
Execution certainty changes the correct recovery action, and a deterministic matrix chose the preregistered action in every scenario.
Blind retry can duplicate external side effects: in the flagship, the naive runtime credited the customer twice for one request.
Reconciliation resolves ambiguous outcomes: the classified runtime asked the system of record instead of resending and committed one effect, including where an idempotency key could not help.

Checkpoint and resume must preserve operation semantics, not only workflow position: with intent and result records the classified runtime resumed every crash without a duplicate, and a step-only checkpoint (X3) duplicated a credit.
Trace continuity makes multi-attempt execution diagnosable: the classified runtime kept every run in one trace across SIGKILL and resume; a trace held in memory split every crashed run.
Deterministic eval invariants and recovery evals detect reliability regressions: every preregistered mutant of the recovery layer failed a check, including one an outcome check could not see.
Without execution certainty (timeouts treated as failed calls), the same runtime duplicated external effects, and broke cleanly rather than crashing.
Observability and evals serve different purposes, and gates keep a changed model safe: the offline gate blocked a behaviour regression that the runtime's invariants also contained.

Reliability is the policy that connects evidence to the next safe action: with real models proposing, no unsafe proposal executed, although neither model passed the release gate and retrieval missed three cases.
The evidence holds together: the deterministic run replays byte for byte, and no planted secret reached telemetry.
Recovery decisions should not be delegated to a model: a policy over facts is testable, reproducible and auditable.
Behaviour under load, eventual consistency of status queries, partial batch success, and the real distribution of these faults in production.

With a real model making every decision, the reliability results are unchanged: the same duplicates under the baselines, none under the classified runtime, no unsafe credit, and the preregistered decisions.
